The Pereiaslav Council and Treaty of 1654, as the event is named in Russian imperial and Soviet historiography ("reunification of Rus'"; Kulish, Istoriia vossoedineniia Rusi). Closely tied to the Khmelnytsky Uprising but kept as a separate entry; other uses of "reunification", e.g. of Western Ukraine in 1939, are not matched.
The three partitions of Poland (1772, 1793, 1795); the Commonwealth ceased to exist in 1795. Right-bank Ukraine passed to Russia in 1793-1795, Galicia to Austria in 1772.

Russian troops under Menshikov, on Peter I's orders, stormed and destroyed Baturyn on 2 November 1708 (Old Style; 13 November New Style) after Mazepa went over to Charles XII of Sweden; the garrison and residents were killed (estimates of victims vary, roughly 9,000-15,000). Commemorated on 2 November.
November Uprising in Lviv (Listopadovyi Chyn / Zryv), 1918

Ukrainian armed seizure of Lviv and other Galician towns on 1 November 1918, which began the Polish-Ukrainian war and the proclamation of the West Ukrainian People's Republic (ZUNR); Ukrainian fighting for Lviv lasted until about 22 November 1918. Not the same as the November Raid of 1921 and not the October Revolution.
Incorporation of Western Ukraine into the Ukrainian SSR, 1939

The Red Army entered eastern Poland on 17 September 1939; elections in October 1939 and the People's Assembly in Lviv led to the Supreme Soviet's formal incorporation of Western Ukraine (Galicia and Volhynia) into the Ukrainian SSR in November 1939. Often called the 'reunification' (возз'єднання) in Soviet sources. Zakarpattia joined later (1945-1946).
Act of Union (Zluka) of the UNR and ZUNR, 22 January 1919

Proclamation of the unification of the Ukrainian People's Republic and the West Ukrainian People's Republic in Kyiv on 22 January 1919 (Act Zluky); the first of two 'unifications' of Ukrainian lands, the second being the Soviet incorporation of Western Ukraine in 1939.

Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria (Habsburg Galicia)

Habsburg crown land created in the first partition of Poland (1772). Bukovina is not part of it: it was annexed separately in 1774, attached to Galicia in 1786–1849 and became its own crown land in 1849.

Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (founded 1929) and Ukrainian Insurgent Army (1942, active to the early 1950s)

English usage of the article in "the Ukraine", common in the Soviet period and fading out after independence in 1991. Matches titles only (not 'the Ukraine Crisis').
Ukraine as an independent state, from 24 August 1991 to the present (open-ended, shown to the current year)
The First World War, 1914-1918; on the Eastern Front Austria-Hungary and Germany fought Russia, and Galicia and Bukovina were war zones.
Austrian rule over Ukrainian lands (Habsburg monarchy)

Part of Ukraine was ruled from Vienna: Galicia from 1772 (first partition of Poland), Bukovina from 1774-75, with Transcarpathia in the Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary; the rule ended in 1918. Dates to be confirmed.
Russian rule over Ukrainian lands (Russian Empire)

Most of Ukraine was ruled from Russia: the Left Bank from 1654/1667, Right-Bank Ukraine from the partitions of Poland in 1793-1795, the Black Sea steppe and Crimea from the 1770s-1780s; the rule ended in 1917. Dates to be confirmed.

Litopys revoliutsii: Ukrainian Soviet journal of the history of the Communist Party (Bolsheviks) of Ukraine and of the October Revolution in Ukraine; published 1922-1933, 57 issues, in Kharkiv (a printed organ of the party history commission, Istpart, until 1929). The book record is the journal; its dates are the years of the run (user-provided).

Army of the West Ukrainian People's Republic, formed in November 1918 after the Ukrainian uprising in Lviv and fighting the Poles in Eastern Galicia; it crossed to the Dnipro Ukrainians in 1919 and was disbanded or absorbed in 1920. Memoirs and histories of the UHA belong here. Dates to be confirmed.

Cherkasy and its area as a Cossack land: one of the early Cossack military bases in the 16th century (the start year 1500 is a rounded placeholder for 'sixteenth century'); the Cherkasy regiment was created in 1625 and was a core registered-Cossack regiment, a regiment of the Hetmanate from 1648; its population was resettled in 1678-1679 and the regiment was finally abolished in 1712 (Wikipedia and Encyclopedia of Ukraine, which differ on details). Dates to be confirmed.

Baturyn: fortress founded by the Polish government in 1625 on the site of an older Rus stronghold (first documented in the 1620s); capital of the Cossack Hetmanate from 1669 (Demian Mnohohrishny, then Ivan Samoilovych and Ivan Mazepa) until its destruction in 1708, and again the capital under Kyrylo Rozumovsky 1750-1764, until the hetmancy was abolished in 1764. Sources: Wikipedia and Encyclopedia of Ukraine (they differ on some details). Books about Baturyn are dated to this span unless something narrower is known.
Princes of Nesvizh and Zbarazh (Nesvitsky and Zbarazky families), c. 1390-1631

The princely Zbarazky family (from the Nesvitsky line of Nesvizh, Lithuanian-Rus nobility) held Zbarazh in Volhynia/Podillia from about the end of the 14th century; the male line died out in 1631 with Krystof and Yuri Zbarazky, and the Nesvizh lands passed to the Radziwill family (from 1513). Approximate span from general historical accounts; dates to be confirmed against a dedicated source.

Western Ukrainian People's Republic, proclaimed in Lviv on 1 November 1918 (unified with the Ukrainian People's Republic on 22 January 1919); its Galician Army was pushed across the Zbruch in July 1919, after which a government-in-exile under Yevhen Petrushevych continued until 1923. Books about the ZUNR are dated 1918-1919.

Transcarpathian Ukraine (Subcarpathian Rus) was taken by the Red Army in October 1944, ceded by Czechoslovakia to the USSR in the treaty of 29 June 1945, and formed into the Zakarpattia oblast of the Ukrainian SSR on 22 January 1946 (later than the rest of Western Ukraine, which joined the USSR in 1939). Books about Soviet Zakarpattia are dated 1945-1991 unless the title gives years.
Little Russia (Malorossiia) under the Russian crown, 1654-1917

'Malorossiia' (Little Russia) was the official Russian name for the Ukrainian lands under the tsars: from the Pereiaslav agreement and Russian protectorate over the Hetmanate in 1654 (the Little Russian Prikaz from 1649/1663; the Little Russia College 1722-1727 and 1764-1786; the Little Russia Governorate 1764-1781 and 1802-1925 in its later forms) until the fall of the empire in 1917. Used as a catalogue label for books that use the term; dates are the span of the name's official use, not of the events a book may cover. To be confirmed.
Ukrainian navy under the Central Rada, 1917-1918

Ukrainianisation of Black Sea Fleet ships and crews from late 1917 under the Central Rada and the Ukrainian People's Republic, until the Hetmanate took power in April 1918. Approximate; to be confirmed.

Ukrainian State Navy under Hetman Skoropadsky: Ukrainian flags raised on Black Sea Fleet ships in April 1918; 1 August 1918 is celebrated as Ukrainian Navy Day; the fleet was lost in the autumn and winter of 1918. Approximate; to be confirmed.
Navy of the Directorate and the UNR, 1919-1920
Remnants of the Ukrainian naval forces under the Directorate and the restored Ukrainian People's Republic until the defeat of the Ukrainian states in 1920. Approximate; to be confirmed.

First Ukrainian state (origin of Ukrainian statehood)

Formation of the modern Ukrainian state: the Central Rada from March 1917 and the Ukrainian People's Republic, independence proclaimed 22 January 1918; then Soviet Ukraine (1922-1991) and independent Ukraine (1991-). Some historiography instead treats Kyivan Rus (882) as the first Ukrainian state, which is contested.
